title: Who's Really Teaching Helplessness?
author: Caiti Wade
summary: Caiti Wade tackles the popular critique that explicit instruction creates learned helplessness by arguing the criticism inverts the actual mechanism: learned helplessness is produced not by too much support but by repeated failure with no path to success. Using a personal camping analogy, she illustrates how appropriate scaffolding—tailored, temporary, and aimed at eventual removal—is what enables people to attempt difficult things in the first place. Both throwing students into the deep end and lowering the bar to the point of meaninglessness communicate the same message—'this isn't for you'—and both are more likely to produce helplessness than well-designed explicit instruction. Independence is not the absence of instruction; it is what happens after good instruction.
points: The common claim that explicit instruction creates learned helplessness inverts the psychology: learned helplessness results from repeated failure with no effective path forward, not from receiving support.
Two opposite failures—throwing students in the deep end and lowering the bar to nothing—both communicate 'this isn't for you' and both are more likely to produce avoidance than independence.
Scaffolded camping as an analogy: the author only attempted camping because it was made accessible through temporary support, which is exactly the purpose of instructional scaffolding.

True independence is the outcome of good instruction, not the precondition for it; removing scaffolds prematurely for ideological reasons produces the despair that gets mislabeled as independence-building.
The archivist notes this piece addresses a live debate in evidence-informed teaching circles about whether structured, teacher-led instruction undermines student agency.
quotes: There's a common criticism that explicit instruction creates learned helplessness by providing too much support. But if learned helplessness is the belief that your efforts won't lead to success, we should ask a different question. Who's really teaching helplessness?
Learned helplessness is not produced by too much support. It is produced by repeated failure with no path to success.

Sometimes we throw students into the deep end in the name of independence and watch them flounder. Other times, convinced they'll never be able to access the core curriculum, we lower the bar altogether and replace meaningful learning with tasks designed simply to keep them occupied. Both approaches teach the same lesson: this isn't for you.
True independence is not the absence of instruction. It is what happens after good instruction.
The goal of scaffolding is always eventual removal—but the removal has to be earned by demonstrated mastery, not imposed prematurely by ideology.
